authors.name: Rowan Vale
authors.bio: The man behind The Pecking Order. Rowan trades in sharp verdicts, spectacular reversals and an unwavering belief that this week finally explained everything. His inbox rarely agrees.

authors.name: Mara Voss
authors.bio: Mara follows the details that outlast the scoreboard: protection, personnel, responsibility and the choices that turn a talented roster into a contender.

authors.name: Ellis Quill
authors.bio: Ellis writes The Long Season, a column about the people and expectations beneath the standings. A bad afternoon is evidence, not a complete biography.

authors.name: Dorian Pike
authors.bio: Dorian asks the awkward question, counts the points and keeps asking. The Uncomfortable Truth takes the league’s overlooked clubs seriously.

authors.name: Tessa Wren
authors.bio: Tessa studies the matchups, names the pressure points and puts a score beside every pick. She covers the entire weekly slate for The Week Ahead.

authors.name: Calvin Rook
authors.bio: Calvin covers the college game and the next IFL class. The Rook Board is built around projection, athletic traits and the occasional prospect he refuses to stop believing in.

articles.title: Five for Accel: Mossdeep turns a tied game into 63–10
articles.dek: Accel BeckhmJr caught five touchdowns and Dram Marino threw six as the unbeaten Eclipse overwhelmed Lavender before their bye.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Lavender had its answer ready. Mossdeep scored, Mr. Clanky took the kickoff back 100 yards, and for a few minutes the Wails had turned the league's most productive offense into one half of a tied game. That was the last time the afternoon belonged to both teams. The Eclipse scored the next 21 points before halftime and finished a 63–10 victory with Accel BeckhmJr collecting five receiving touchdowns.

Eight catches. Ten targets. Two hundred and thirty-three yards. BeckhmJr needed all of one touchdown to put Mossdeep ahead 28–7 before the break, then added four more in a second-half stretch that made every Lavender possession feel urgently short. The Eclipse are 7–0, have scored 307 points and will spend Week 8 on a bye. The Wails are 4–2 and have Blackthorn next. Travis Scarboro has a very different week to prepare.
I was going to count them on one hand, then remembered the ball was still coming. Dram made the hard part look suspiciously easy. Ask him about that.
body.speaker: Accel BeckhmJr

body.text: Dram Marino's contribution was substantial enough to survive the joke. The Drampa completed 22 of 28 passes for 381 yards, six touchdowns and no interceptions. He found eight different receivers. Gronkaludon caught all five of his targets for 43 yards, and Marshall Flock turned his only reception into a 12-yard touchdown. Mossdeep's quarterback now has 22 passing scores against two interceptions through seven games. Michael Dorrill's attack is giving defenses several problems before the most spectacular one arrives.
A tie that did not last

Ninjaskamara opened the scoring on a ten-yard run left with 3:33 remaining in the first quarter. Adam Vinathorn converted, then kicked off to Mr. Clanky. The Iron Bundle returned it 100 yards for Lavender's only touchdown; the extra point made it 7–7. It was an enormous special-teams response from a player whose passing afternoon would become increasingly difficult.

Lavender could not turn that burst into sustained offense. Mr. Clanky finished 12 of 34 for 102 yards with two interceptions. The Wails produced eight first downs and 161 total yards. Mossdeep finished with 18 and 531. A return touchdown counts every bit as much as a long offensive drive, but it does not solve the next third down, and the Wails converted only four of eleven.

Ninjaskamara scored again with 5:18 left in the second quarter, taking a seven-yard run left into the end zone. Marino later threw deep right to Flock for the 12-yard score with 2:06 remaining. Mossdeep was moving the ball with a lead, a running threat and several passing destinations available. Lavender was already being asked to create another exceptional response.

The Wails did make Marino uncomfortable on individual snaps. Grimace Shake sacked him twice, including a six-yard loss with 39 seconds left before halftime. That brought up third-and-eleven. Marino immediately answered with a short-left throw to BeckhmJr for a 14-yard touchdown at 0:21. A defensive success had created the down Lavender wanted. The next play still ended in the end zone.
After the sack, the distance was the thing to settle. Accel gave me a throw I could finish. I don't want the six touchdowns to hide how many ordinary catches kept us moving.
body.speaker: Dram Marino

body.text: Four scores, both sides of the field

Lavender's 29-yard field goal with 3:38 remaining in the third quarter brought the score to 28–10. Ninjaskamara answered later with his third rushing touchdown, a four-yard run up the middle at 0:34. His final rushing line was 19 carries for 90 yards; he also caught a 39-yard pass. A minor injury appears in the game report, with no remaining absence listed in the current injury report.

Then the takeaways and BeckhmJr's routes began arriving together. Derrat Brooks intercepted a deep-right throw with 17 seconds left in the third and returned it 14 yards. Six seconds later, Marino threw deep right to BeckhmJr for a 35-yard touchdown. Mossdeep took a 42–10 lead into the fourth quarter, and Lavender's attempts to chase the game were now handing the Eclipse additional chances.

BeckhmJr scored from 39 yards on a short-left pass at 5:14. Clay Rathews intercepted Mr. Clanky's next deep-right attempt at 4:55, returning it 18 yards. At 4:30, Marino went deep right to BeckhmJr for a 30-yard touchdown. At 4:03, they connected deep left for 55 more. Three fourth-quarter scores, in a span of 71 seconds on the game clock, took a rout to 63 points.

Those descriptions matter. BeckhmJr's touchdowns were not all deep throws and they did not all attack the same side. Short left produced scores of 14 and 39 yards; deep right produced 35 and 30; deep left supplied 55. The receiving totals show the damage. The sequence shows why Lavender never found a comfortable place to defend it.
The work beneath the headline

Mossdeep converted eight of ten third downs and punted once. Flock added 42 rushing yards on five carries to his touchdown catch. Gronkaludon's five receptions and the catches by Travis Meltce, Lorenzo Steel and Ninjulio Jones kept Marino's distribution wider than the five-touchdown headline suggests. Vinathorn made all nine extra points. There was very little wasted finishing work.

The defense forced two interceptions and broke up ten passes in the team comparison. Shawn Mareman, the defensive player of the game, had a sack, a pass defended and six pressures in his individual line. Luvrelle Revis recorded three passes defended. The Wails' best offensive receiving total belonged to Beedrill, with three catches for 39 yards. Mr. Clanky's return was remarkable; Lavender needed far more of the possessions after it.

For Scarboro, the next opponent offers no gentle reset. Blackthorn just beat Lavaridge 42–0 and sits 5–1. Lavender remains in the playoff picture, but its record now comes with 78 points scored and 130 allowed. The response has to begin with possessions that let its defense rest and a passing game that can survive without a return touchdown doing the scoring.

Mossdeep gets a week without a game and a receiver whose season totals have jumped to 24 catches, 568 yards and ten touchdowns. Half those touchdowns came here. The last was the 55-yarder to the left, after Lavender had already been hurt to the right and underneath. By then, BeckhmJr had run out of new ways to count them.

articles.title: Four kicks, then four incompletions: Cerulean makes twelve enough
articles.dek: Grotle supplied every Tide point. The defense finished a 12–6 upset by denying Sunyshore four straight throws on its final possession.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Cerulean won the part of this game that happened after Sunyshore seemed to have found its answer. Three consecutive completions moved the Starseekers 53 yards on their final possession. Then came four incompletions, two broken up by Carnivine and one by Maractus. A 12–6 win required all four stops. The Tide made them, and Grotle’s four field goals suddenly looked like a sufficient offensive plan.

Sunyshore had scored first, on DeZhaun Watzon’s one-yard run up the middle with 2:10 remaining in the opening quarter. The extra point missed. That single touchdown stood as the Starseekers’ entire scoring return, despite two late possessions that could have changed the result. Karson Jones’s team fell to 5–2. Cerulean improved to 4–3, with a win that will make its bye week rather easier to enjoy.

The useful distinction is how each passing game handled the ordinary work. Farigiraf completed 23 of 37 throws for 197 yards without an interception or a sack. Watzon finished 10-for-26 for 125, threw an interception and took three sacks. Neither quarterback threw a touchdown. One gave his kicker enough opportunities to score four times; the other spent much of the afternoon trying to recover from possessions that had gone nowhere.
Four is a nice number when all four go through. I wasn’t standing there wishing we needed a more interesting kick. Twenty-four yards suits me fine.
body.speaker: Grotle

body.text: Grotle began with a 25-yarder at the opening of the second quarter, finishing a possession that had covered 59 yards. His 40-yarder with 1:54 left in the half tied the game at six. A 36-yarder with two seconds remaining put Cerulean ahead. The fourth, from 24 yards with 1:48 left in the third, set the final margin. There was no long-distance rescue here. Cerulean repeatedly brought him into usable range, and he finished every assignment.
The interception bought three points

The second kick followed Vikavolt’s interception of Watzon’s deep-right pass at 3:04 in the second quarter. Vikavolt returned it 21 yards. Cerulean then gained 16 yards on the ensuing possession before Grotle tied the score. That is a modest amount of offense, but a meaningful exchange in a game where every scoring chance mattered. Sunyshore had given the Tide a shorter route to three points.

Pressure supplied a different form of disruption. Watchog sacked Watzon for a six-yard loss in the second quarter. Chesnaught added losses of eight and five in the third. Cerulean recorded three sacks while allowing none. The difference did not produce a spectacular defensive touchdown; it helped make an afternoon of unsuccessful drives possible. Sunyshore converted two of nine third downs and punted five times.

The Tide were hardly strolling down the field themselves. They ran 21 times for only 28 yards and also punted five times. Seismitoad’s eleven carries produced seventeen yards. The answer came through short gains in the passing game: Arctozolt caught six of seven targets for 57 yards, Delcatty added six catches for 49, and Watchog caught four for 40. Cerulean converted six of sixteen third downs. It needed persistence because explosive offense was in short supply.

For Misty, that balance was enough to create four scoring possessions without asking the running game to become something it was not. The Tide finished with 225 yards to Sunyshore’s 207. The eighteen-yard gap was small; the difference in wasted opportunities was larger. Cerulean lost no fumbles and threw no interceptions. Sunyshore lost one of each.
Two chances, two different failures

The fumble arrived late enough to look decisive. With 2:03 remaining in the fourth quarter, Scol Alexander ran left for a two-yard loss and lost the ball. Shellder recovered for Cerulean. Sunyshore had moved 57 yards on that possession before it ended. A team chasing six points cannot assume the next chance will arrive after giving one away so close to the finish.

It did arrive. Cerulean could not drain the game, and Grotle punted with 1:54 left. Watzon hit Floatzel short right for six yards, then Sceptile short right for 21, then Floatzel deep left for 26. Those three throws briefly supplied exactly the passing rhythm missing for most of the afternoon. Sunyshore was threatening again, with enough time to complete the task.

The final four throws went to four successive situations with the same result. Carnivine broke up attempts to MF STOMP short right and deep right. Maractus denied a deep-left pass to FIN FANG FOOM. On fourth-and-ten, the short-right attempt to Frigibax fell incomplete with 1:09 remaining. Farigiraf took over for two kneels. Cerulean had survived the recovery from its own failure to close the game a possession earlier.
We found three good throws, and then I needed another one. It’s a very small number until the whole game is asking you for it.
body.speaker: DeZhaun Watzon

body.text: The game’s injury list marked Myles Gabite and Scol Alexander with minor issues. Neither entry supplies an explanation for the sequence of missed chances, and neither should replace the visible football. Sunyshore gets Mahogany next. The immediate repair is straightforward to describe and harder to perform: more completed throws before the final possession, fewer lost opportunities after a drive has begun to work.

Cerulean can carry a simpler memory into its bye. Its offense did not reach the end zone, its defense did not surrender a point after the first quarter, and its kicker missed nothing. When the lead was finally tested by three sharp completions, Carnivine and Maractus put their hands on the answer.

articles.title: Porygon-Z finds the second-half answer for unbeaten Mt. Silver
articles.dek: Porygon-Z threw two second-half touchdowns, Tony Gyarzalez reached 100 yards, and Mt. Silver rallied past Petalburg 17–14 to reach 7–0.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Mt. Silver’s seventh win required a scoreless first half, a long throw to a familiar tight end, and a quarterback who finished with the ball from an onside kick. Porygon-Z wore No. 8 and supplied the full passing line: 21 completions on 33 attempts, 223 yards and two touchdowns. The Reds beat Petalburg 17–14. Their record stayed perfect while their season continued to change around it.

A week ago, Crem Ftzpatrik’s relief appearance had become the immediate answer after Josh Alakazam was lost for the season. This game belonged to Porygon-Z. There is no need to make the transition more mysterious or more tidy than the football itself. Connor McLarren needed a productive afternoon from the quarterback on the field. He got one, eventually, after Petalburg had spent an entire half making the new assignment uncomfortable.

The Pride led 7–0 at halftime. Iron Valiant had found Golbat short left for a six-yard touchdown with 1:54 left in the first quarter, and Petalburg’s defense protected that lead through a second quarter in which neither team scored. Delcatty sacked Porygon-Z twice before the break. A 76-yard Reds possession ended on downs. Mt. Silver had movement, but no points to show for it.
Tony kept giving me somewhere useful to throw it. I’m happy to let everybody admire the hundred yards. I was mostly pleased he kept being available.
body.speaker: Porygon-Z

body.text: Tony Gyarzalez finished with five catches for 100 yards. The one that changed the shape of the afternoon arrived early in the third quarter: third-and-ten, 5:50 on the clock, a deep-right pass that went for 59 yards. After a half spent assembling gains without a scoring finish, the Reds had crossed a large piece of the field in one throw. Flygon made the tackle, leaving Mt. Silver more work to do.
Seventeen points after the break

Petalburg still resisted. Delcatty recorded a third sack, again for seven yards, with 4:44 left in the third quarter. The Reds eventually settled for Adam Venutieri’s 28-yard field goal at 4:21. It cut the lead to 7–3. That was a successful defensive stand after the long completion, but it was also the first time Mt. Silver had received any payment for its offensive work.

The next scoring possession finished differently. Porygon-Z found Gregar Jenings short left for eight yards on third-and-eight with 1:01 remaining in the third. The touchdown and extra point made it 10–7. On a later drive in the fourth, Scep Smith Jr. caught a three-yard touchdown, again on a short-left throw, with 3:55 left. The Reds had scored seventeen unanswered points, using the long completion to begin the recovery and shorter throws to finish it.

Gyarzalez did not score. Plusico Buress did not score either, though his six catches for 45 yards supplied a substantial part of the ordinary work between the larger moments. The pair accounted for eleven of Porygon-Z’s 21 completions. I tend to trust that kind of distribution more than a story in which a new quarterback supposedly becomes self-sufficient overnight. There were useful receivers accepting their share of the afternoon.
The long one helped us. So did the next short catch. When we were behind, I wanted us to keep seeing the whole field and the whole game. There was still time.
body.speaker: Tony Gyarzalez

body.text: Raticate carried nine times for 48 yards, and Vibrava added 43 on six attempts. Mt. Silver finished with 89 rushing yards, including the two late kneels that reduced the total. With Garshawn Lynch still out, the supporting runners again supplied enough movement to keep the offense from becoming entirely about its quarterback. That is a continuing responsibility, not a one-game favor.

Petalburg’s offense had its own productive runner. Oinkologne gained 62 yards on eleven carries and caught both targets for another 26. Iron Valiant completed seventeen of 29 passes for 157 yards, with two touchdowns and no interceptions. The Pride finished with 244 total yards. They were competitive enough to lead, then competitive enough to make Mt. Silver finish the game properly after losing that lead.
The last recovery belonged to the quarterback

Blaziken supplied both Reds sacks, for losses of seven and eight yards. The second came with 2:14 left in the fourth quarter, on the possession Petalburg was using to chase a ten-point deficit. The Pride kept going. On fourth-and-five at the two-minute mark, Iron Valiant threw short left to Girafarig for a fourteen-yard touchdown. The extra point made it 17–14. A comfortable ending had disappeared.

Porygon-Z recovered Sunflora’s onside kick. That is an unusual sentence to place near the center of a quarterback’s afternoon, but it was a vital piece of this one. Petalburg needed the ball back, and Mt. Silver kept it. Vibrava then contributed a ten-yard run left and a twelve-yard reception short left before Porygon-Z took the final kneels. The offense that had been scoreless for half the game handled the closing responsibility.

Petalburg lost one fumble, on Whiscash’s three-yard reception with 28 seconds remaining in the second quarter; Mienfoo recovered it. Mt. Silver did not turn that chance into points before the break. The Reds lost no fumbles and threw no interceptions themselves. The difference mattered over the full afternoon even when an individual recovery did not immediately improve the scoreboard.

The injury report still leaves McLarren with substantial work: Alakazam is out for the season, Lynch has four weeks remaining, and the Reds have Snowpoint next. Petalburg falls to 5–2 and goes into its bye with a narrow loss to an unbeaten opponent. Neither team needs an exaggerated lesson from three points. The Reds have earned seven wins; the Pride made this one difficult enough to be worth remembering.

For Mt. Silver, the clearest memory may be the quarterback holding an onside kick while his team protected a three-point lead. There was still a run, a pass and two kneels to complete. Porygon-Z and the Reds completed them.

art.alt: Mt. Silver quarterback Porygon-Z No. 8 in red and silver.

articles.title: Rustboro owned the yardage. Vivillon took the lead.
articles.dek: Azalea erased a 10–0 halftime deficit, won on a 50-yard pass and stopped Rustboro’s last fourth down to claim a 14–10 comeback.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Rustboro accumulated 334 yards, nineteen first downs and plenty of material for an extremely unconvincing explanation of why it lost. Azalea accumulated the final fourteen points. Vivillon’s fifty-yard touchdown catch with 2:38 remaining put the Swarm ahead, and Kricketune’s stop on fourth-and-five preserved a 14–10 victory. There is a reason the largest numbers in the game report are printed beside the team names.

The Stone led 10–0 at halftime and did not score again. Their first three possessions traveled 76, 64 and 69 yards. Those drives produced a touchdown, a field goal and a lost fumble. Azalea had almost no margin for another early concession, and Crabrawler’s recovery near the end of the half kept the comeback small enough to remain practical. Rustboro had done a great deal of work without making the game safe.

Philly supplied the first touchdown, running up the middle for three yards on third-and-one with 1:43 left in the opening quarter. Gorebyss added the extra point, then a 31-yard field goal with 2:57 remaining in the second. The Stone were moving the ball patiently and repeatedly. At that stage, another scoring drive looked more plausible than a second half in which none of them would pay off.
The yards were there. I’m not going to argue with the part where we needed more points. Keeping the ball at the end of that run would have helped us do that.
body.speaker: My Way, Son

body.text: My Way, Son ran for 109 yards on eighteen carries, a useful afternoon by almost every conventional rushing measure. With 23 seconds left before halftime, however, the Iron Treads gained nine yards on a run left and fumbled. Crabrawler recovered for Azalea. Last week, two 94-yard kickoff touchdowns had helped make My Way, Son the story of Rustboro’s win at Dewford. This week the decisive special contribution was missing, and one ordinary rushing mistake carried a much larger bill.
The comeback took two different routes

Azalea did not immediately transform the reprieve into a smooth offense. Its first possession after halftime covered 72 yards and ended on downs. Rustboro’s defense had protected the ten-point lead through another long drive. The Swarm had to get the ball back and begin again, which is less convenient than the usual comeback montage but considerably closer to what happened.

Zoroark helped by sacking Porygon-Z for five yards at 3:20 in the third quarter. Rustboro punted after gaining only two yards on that possession. Azalea’s next drive traveled forty yards and finished with Mienfoo running up the middle for a fifteen-yard touchdown on third-and-two, with eighteen seconds remaining in the quarter. Sunflora’s extra point cut the lead to 10–7. Now the Stone’s lost opportunities had a visible price.

Mienfoo carried only twice, for 22 yards. Beedrill handled the larger rushing workload, twelve carries for 56. The contrast is useful: Azalea needed its regular gains, and it also needed the less frequent runner to finish a particular chance. The Swarm produced 84 rushing yards overall, well behind Rustboro’s 150. They used one of those runs to put seven points on the board when the game was beginning to run out.

Rustboro then drove 53 yards and turned the ball over on downs. Azalea took over and moved 75 yards in five plays. The final fifty came when Drampa threw deep right to Vivillon with 2:38 left. It was the only touchdown pass of the game, and it changed the leader. Sunflora’s extra point made it 14–10. The Swarm had spent most of the afternoon chasing; now Rustboro needed a touchdown.
I knew we needed the catch. Once it was mine, I wanted the whole play. There wasn’t much to say afterward. I was looking at the score.
body.speaker: Vivillon

body.text: Vivillon finished with four catches on six targets for 96 yards. Drampa completed twelve of 22 passes for 176 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions. Those are not the numbers of an offense that dominated every exchange. They are the numbers of an offense that stayed close enough for its best passing play to decide the lead. Bugsy’s team had given itself one good opportunity to make a dramatic fact out of a fairly modest passing day.
The Stone had one more long drive

Rustboro’s final possession again made progress. On third-and-eleven with 1:56 remaining, Porygon-Z found Gengar deep right for 25 yards. Lombre later caught a six-yard pass short right. Watchog converted a fourth-and-one with a run up the middle. The Stone kept extending the argument, and Azalea kept being required to answer another snap. A team can lose this kind of game by assuming the previous good stop was the last one it needed.

With 1:02 left, Rustboro faced fourth-and-five. My Way, Son ran left and gained nothing; Kricketune made the tackle. That was the end of the Stone’s last scoring opportunity. Azalea still needed to close the game, and Drampa’s fifteen-yard completion short right to Hippopotas with 57 seconds remaining helped provide the final answer before a kneel. The Swarm had won both the explosive-play contest and the last necessary small exchange.

Gengar caught five passes for eighty yards for Rustboro. Porygon-Z completed eighteen of 32 for 184 yards, without a touchdown or an interception. The Stone converted six of twelve third downs and ran 64 plays to Azalea’s forty. Tyler Scarboro has enough evidence of movement here to resist declaring the whole offense broken. He also has a second-half zero that will not improve by being surrounded with favorable statistics.

Both clubs are now 3–4. Rustboro visits Viridian next; Azalea hosts Cianwood. The Swarm will have to account for Scraggy’s two-week absence after a game in which he recorded a sack. Rustboro still has Parasect unavailable for four weeks. Those are next week’s problems. This week ended when a team with more yards needed five more and Kricketune allowed none.

art.alt: Azalea receiver Vivillon No. 11 with a football.

articles.title: Sunyshore had two chances. Stop arguing about the twelve points.
articles.dek: Mara Voss follows the last two Starseekers possessions and finds a defeat that cannot be explained by four opposing field goals.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I don't want to hear that Sunyshore lost because Cerulean kicked four field goals. Of course the Tide kicked four field goals. Grotle made every attempt, the Starseekers scored six points, and arithmetic remains undefeated. Karson Jones needs a more useful conversation. His defense kept offering the offense a way out of a bad afternoon. Twice in the fourth quarter, Sunyshore moved the ball far enough to make that invitation serious. Twice, the possession ended without points.

That's where I'd start the meeting. At 3:36 remaining, trailing 12–6, Sunyshore began a possession that would cover 57 yards. After a fumble ended it, the defense immediately forced a punt. The next possession moved rapidly through three completed passes before failing on downs. Those are two distinct opportunities. Filing the entire loss under a vague complaint about offensive rhythm would let too many decisions escape inspection.

The first deserves particular attention because Sunyshore briefly found several different ways to advance. DeZhaun Watzon threw short middle to Swampert for ten yards. On third-and-one, a deep-right pass toward Floatzel was broken up by Raticate. Myles Gabite then took a fourth-and-one run left for eight. Scol Alexander ran up the middle for five and left for sixteen. The offense had a productive response to a failed throw. Good. Keep that part.

Then came the costly finish. Watzon completed a deep-right pass to Frigibax for nineteen yards. With 2:03 left, Scol Alexander ran left, lost two yards and fumbled. Shellder recovered for Cerulean. I won't invent a missed blocking assignment or announce that the ball carrier should have foreseen a particular tackle. The recorded sequence gives us enough: an offense finally joining its running and passing gains together lost the ball on first down.
It felt like finding the right door and dropping the key down the drain. We got another key, too. That part makes it harder to shrug at.
body.speaker: DeZhaun Watzon

body.text: The defense returned the favor

Cerulean took over with 2:02 remaining. Seismitoad lost a yard on a run right, lost another up the middle and then caught a short-right pass for two. Donphan made both rushing tackles; Vigoroth finished the reception. Grotle punted. That is a clean, useful defensive answer to a turnover. Sunyshore's offense had scarcely finished being disappointed before it was being asked to try again.

This is why I'm impatient with treating the result as a single blur of frustration. The Tide won without an offensive touchdown. Sunyshore held them to 28 rushing yards on 21 attempts. A defense can still make mistakes in a game like that, and Cerulean did convert six of sixteen third downs. But the final stop arrived exactly when it was needed. Jones had a game to win after the fumble.

At 1:47, Watzon found Floatzel short right for six. Three seconds later he hit Sceptile short right for 21. At 1:33, he went deep left to Floatzel for 26. Three completed passes, 53 yards before the ensuing failures, and a very different picture from the offense's earlier procession of punts. If you want evidence that this group could move against Cerulean, there it is. Nobody needs to borrow it from last week's score.

The next four throws were incomplete. Carnivine broke up consecutive passes intended for Swampert, the first short right and the second deep right. Maractus broke up the third-down deep-left attempt toward Finizen. The fourth-down short-right throw toward Frigibax also failed. Cerulean took over with 1:06 left and knelt twice. That is the end of the argument about whether there was still time.

I see a defense repeatedly contesting the catch, not a mystery that can be solved by yelling for more effort. Sunyshore finished ten of twenty-six passing, with three sacks and an interception. The Tide swatted nine passes. The final series supplied three named breakups in a row before the last incompletion. Any preparation for Mahogany that doesn't make those contested throws a central subject is missing the most legible evidence in the game.
Don't throw away the parts that worked

The temptation after six points is to declare every offensive choice defective. I wouldn't. Sunyshore ran for 82 yards on sixteen attempts. Myles Gabite's fourth-down conversion kept that first late drive alive. Scol Alexander's sixteen-yard run mattered before his fumble mattered. A ball-security correction should preserve the fact that the running game gave the offense useful distances and genuine progress.

Nor would I pretend every deep pass was reckless. Floatzel's 26-yard catch helped build the last chance. Frigibax's nineteen-yard reception helped build the previous one. The problem is deciding which opportunities remain sound when the defense is already getting hands on so many throws. That is a question for Jones and Watzon to answer with specific routes and protections in practice, rather than a blanket instruction to become more adventurous or more cautious.

Cerulean deserves credit for the less dramatic work, too. Farigiraf was not sacked. The Tide did not throw an interception or lose a fumble. Grotle connected from 25, forty, 36 and 24 yards. A team that protects its possessions and takes every available kick can beat a more celebrated opponent without producing the afternoon's loudest play. Misty's club moved above .500 at 4–3 by doing precisely that.

Sunyshore remains 5–2, with 181 points scored and 92 allowed. I'm not tearing up that record because one afternoon went sour. I am rejecting the idea that a good season makes the final two possessions unimportant. Contenders need a response more exact than reassurance. They need to retain the gains, correct the failures and know which of those two categories each play belongs in.

Mahogany arrives next. The Frost just protected a one-point lead by finishing their last possession with consecutive productive runs before kneeling. Sunyshore has its own closing sequence to repair. Put four clips next to the 53 yards that preceded them: broken up, broken up, broken up, incomplete. Start there.

art.alt: Pat Serptain, Serperior No. 39, in Sunyshore colors.

articles.title: Close is a score. It is not a diagnosis.
articles.dek: Ellis Quill visits four narrow defeats and argues that the next useful question depends on how each team lost its last chance.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: I have a modest objection to the phrase “one play away.” It is usually true, which makes it very convenient. A team loses by one, two, three or four points, and everyone can select a moment that would have changed the answer. The phrase then sits comfortably between disappointment and hope, asking almost nothing of either. After this week's games, I'd rather ask what the team has to practice.

Rustboro lost by four. Petalburg lost by three. Celadon lost by two. Fortree lost by one. That is a tidy little staircase, although I doubt any of the coaches would appreciate the design. The scores suggest four clubs standing near the same door. The possessions tell a more useful story. They have arrived there by different routes, and some have quite different reasons for being unable to open it.

Start with Rustboro, because Tyler Scarboro's team has plenty of evidence that the basic work of moving the ball was possible. The Stone gained 334 yards against Azalea's 260. They made nineteen first downs to eleven and converted six of twelve third downs. My Way, Son ran for 109 yards. Anyone announcing that the offense could do nothing is going to have an awkward conversation with the first three quarters.

Yet Rustboro scored ten points, all before halftime. Its final two substantial drives ended on downs. With four minutes left, a fourth-and-four short-left pass to Lombre was broken up by Castform. After Azalea went ahead, the Stone returned with another long possession. They converted a fourth-and-one run through Watchog. On the next fourth down, needing five with 1:02 remaining, My Way, Son ran left for no gain. Kricketune made the tackle.
The hundred yards don't cancel that last carry. They also don't disappear because of it. We can work with both things without pretending either one didn't happen.
body.speaker: My Way, Son

body.text: That seems a sensible place for Scarboro to begin. The nine-yard run that ended in a first-half fumble also belongs in the review. Rustboro had enough movement to make several endings painful. The work is to finish those possessions, protect the ball and choose a convincing answer when the distance becomes non-negotiable. “Keep doing everything” is too gentle. “Change everything” would discard the useful parts.
A comeback that never got another turn

Petalburg's 17–14 defeat at Mt. Silver had a different shape. Norman's team reached the end zone on fourth-and-five with two minutes left, Iron Valiant throwing short left to Girafarig for fourteen yards. That was a successful answer at the very moment Rustboro's last drive had lacked one. It gave the Pride a three-point deficit and something worth trying to recover.

The ensuing onside kick went to Mt. Silver. Then Raticate ran right for three, Vibrava ran left for ten and Vibrava caught a short-left pass for twelve. The Reds knelt twice. Petalburg never got to run the next urgent offensive series. It is tempting to spend all the sympathy on the touchdown and all the blame on the kick, but the defensive chance after the recovery matters as well. The Reds still had to collect the yards that ended the contest.

I don't often volunteer applause for Mt. Silver, whose unbeaten record already seems to find sufficient publicity. That final sequence deserves a little. Three different gains, then the quiet finish. For Petalburg, the useful question is how to force the opponent to surrender one more possession. The Pride also punted six times. A late touchdown can be admirable while the preceding work leaves too much for it to solve.

At 5–2, Petalburg can take the bye without turning a three-point loss into an identity crisis. Norman has an offense that produced two passing touchdowns against an unbeaten opponent. He also has specific stretches in which that offense went nowhere. The review needs room for both. I would be wary of any meeting in which the fourth-quarter rally receives all the attention simply because it is easiest to remember kindly.
One point can contain several jobs

Fortree's loss was smaller and its situation more severe. The Skyhawks fell to 0–6 after Chinchou's 53-yard field goal cut Mahogany's lead to 14–13. It was a fine kick. It was also the final time Fortree possessed the ball. When I hear “one point away” in that context, I want to know what happened after the kick, because another successful kick requires another opportunity.

Bibarel ran right for six and then seven. Kricketune followed with runs up the middle for six and ten. Mahogany knelt twice. There is the immediate problem in four ordinary handoffs. Earlier in the quarter, Kingdra had taken consecutive sacks for eight and seven yards, turning an advancing Fortree drive into a punt. Winona has protection to review and a late run defense to repair. The kicker's distance does not make either subject smaller.

Celadon's ending was even longer. The Bloom punted early in the fourth quarter while trailing Canalave 9–7. The Bulwark then held the ball for the remaining 5:12. Grotle converted a fourth-and-one run up the middle for five. Slowking later found Delcatty for ten on third-and-six, then Manectric for eight on second-and-six. Two kneels ended it. Erika never received the last possession that a two-point deficit seems to promise.

The Bloom had managed only six first downs and 167 total yards. Their missed field goal belongs in the explanation, but asking for a better kick cannot be the entire improvement plan. The defense needed one more stop; the offense needed to manufacture more chances before the last five minutes vanished. At 1–6, Celadon needs practical work more than another beautifully phrased reminder of how nearly this one went differently.

These are not four versions of the same football team. Rustboro is 3–4, Petalburg 5–2, Celadon 1–6 and Fortree 0–6. Their next weeks differ, too: the Pride rest, while the Stone visit Viridian, the Bloom visit Fuchsia and the Skyhawks host Vermilion. Encouragement should be specific enough to travel with each team into that next assignment.

I'd tell Rustboro to remember that its last drive reached two fourth downs and answered only one. I'd tell Petalburg that finishing its own touchdown drive still left a defensive job. I'd ask Celadon and Fortree to study the runs and completions that denied them another try. There is hope in close games. There is also a practice schedule. Four yards, three points, two kneels, one more stop: pick the thing your team can actually work on.

articles.title: Blackthorn, keep the ball in Hatterene’s hands.
articles.dek: Dorian Pike counts five touchdown passes, admires an eighty-yard answer to a sack and demands that the Dragons remember what made 42 possible.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: I would like to begin with a respectful acknowledgment of restraint. A club at 5–1 should avoid getting carried away by one emphatic victory. Its coaches should study the mistakes. Its quarterback should thank the blockers. Its receivers should remember that the next game begins at zero. There. The responsible sentences have been completed. Blackthorn won 42–0, Hatterene threw for 410 yards, and I would now like someone to explain why the Dragons should whisper about it.

Five touchdown passes. Thirty completions in 35 attempts. Zero interceptions. Clair's offense gave six different receivers a catch and four different receivers a touchdown. Ninjask had 183 receiving yards; Grovyle caught nine passes. This was a passing game with a devastating lead performer and enough support to keep the entire production from becoming one very long solo.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: the most revealing play came immediately after Blackthorn did something wrong. Hatterene took a sack, leaving second-and-seventeen. With 2:15 left in the second quarter, the next throw went deep middle to Ninjask for an eighty-yard touchdown. Eighty. An offense that can respond to a seven-yard loss by traveling eighty on one completion does not need a lecture about how comforting it would be to run twice and punt politely.

That doesn't excuse the sack. It changes the response available after it. Clair has a quarterback and receiver who turned a bad distance into the afternoon's longest play. I want that confidence to remain part of the plan. If next week's meeting converts a spectacular win into an invitation to become timid, someone should bring the eighty-yard clip and play it at an irritating volume.
Second-and-seventeen sounds wonderfully official. Then Ninjask is running and you start wondering whether the defense filled out the wrong paperwork.
body.speaker: Hatterene

body.text: The short pass joined the argument

The next touchdown to Ninjask traveled 37 yards on a throw described as short middle. It came with 45 seconds left before halftime. This is an important detail for anyone who believes the entire afternoon can be explained by launching the ball farther. The Dragons found an enormous play on a deep throw and another on a short one. The receiver helped turn both into seven points after the conversion.

Ninjask caught seven of eight targets. The eighty-yarder is allowed to attract the spotlight; it has earned the electricity bill. But the seven catches matter because the offense could keep returning to that receiver without requiring every play to be historic. A reliable completion and an explosive finish are pleasant things to find in the same uniform. I recommend that Blackthorn continue taking advantage of the arrangement.

Grovyle supplied nine catches on ten targets for 78 yards. One was the one-yard touchdown that opened the scoring. A receiver who can finish the close work and keep appearing on ordinary downs is doing a different job from the player with the eighty-yard score. Both jobs were necessary to the way this offense distributed its opportunities. The biggest number should not make the other work invisible.

Exploud caught all five targets for 34 yards and a touchdown. Seadra caught both targets for 27 and a touchdown. Furret caught all three for 24. Meganium added four receptions for 64. That is a receiving list with enough names to interrupt the comfortable habit of blaming one matchup for everything. Blackthorn kept finding somewhere useful to put the ball.
The long one counts. So do the catches that give us another set of downs. I'll take the throw that's there and keep running until the play is finished.
body.speaker: Ninjask

body.text: I appreciate the practicality. I also reserve the right to be less calm about eighty yards. Someone on this staff has to enjoy the numbers without immediately wrapping them in a blanket and asking whether they're getting too warm. Ninjask gained more receiving yards than the opposing offense gained total yards. That happened. We can say it at full volume.
A shutout deserves its own paragraph

Several paragraphs, actually. Blackthorn allowed 169 total yards and just 66 through the air. The opposition converted two of eleven third downs and punted seven times. No interception was required to manufacture that shutout. No lost opposing fumble was required either. The Dragons repeatedly made the ordinary defensive sequence work: contest the gain, force the difficult down and get off the field.

Leavanny recorded two sacks. James Harriolu and Beedrill had one each. Politoed made seven tackles, while Whiscash added four and a tackle for loss. A 42-point offense can make every defensive contribution seem like an optional decoration. I object. Those stops helped ensure that Hatterene's success kept widening the game instead of merely answering the next score.

There are corrections available. Blackthorn allowed 103 rushing yards on nineteen carries. Hatterene was sacked three times. The Dragons converted only three of eight third downs and punted three times. Clair can have all those details without surrendering the larger point. Forty-two to nothing is not a fragile result that shatters when somebody mentions a missed opportunity. It can survive inspection.

The protection figures suggest where some of that inspection belongs. Bellibolt allowed five pressures, and Lickilickelce allowed three and a sack. That does not identify every individual assignment on the scoring throws, so I won't pretend it does. It does give the line a concrete subject for work. The quarterback's completion rate should be an achievement the blockers help sustain, not an excuse to ignore the times defenders got through.
Five wins still require a plan

Blackthorn has scored 120 points and allowed 77 across six games. This one result supplied 42 of those points and none of the concessions. That proportion is both exciting and demanding. I cannot honestly promise that this is the offensive output the Dragons will reproduce every week. I can insist that the staff understand exactly which opportunities made it possible before congratulating itself and moving on.

Keep the variety of receiving jobs. Keep the willingness to attack after a setback. Keep the short completions that allow a gifted receiver to make the next defender's afternoon unpleasant. Fix the protection leaks and the wasted third downs. Those instructions can coexist. The idea that ambition and correction must take turns in the same meeting is how good football teams spend too long congratulating themselves on being sensible.

Clair has a 5–1 club and a quarterback who just completed thirty throws. The obligation is to give that quarterback more good decisions to make. When the next second-and-seventeen arrives, remember that Blackthorn has already answered one with Hatterene, Ninjask and eighty yards through the middle.

articles.title: The Rook Board: Dhelmise gets first call, Trubbish gets my attention
articles.dek: Six tight ends, six different buying decisions. Calvin Rook takes Santalune’s strength-and-grade case first, then makes room for a Cascarrafa athlete he wants to keep discussing.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: I am taking Santalune’s Dhelmise first. The 80–99 grade band leads this six-player tight-end class, and 28 bench reps give me a reason to begin the conversation at the line of scrimmage. I can already hear the argument for a faster receiver. Fine. Bring Lavender Forest’s Arctozolt into the room. This is a useful disagreement about what an offense wants its tight end to do, and I have picked the prospect whose present case I find hardest to ignore.

Week 7 made the position easy to explain. Tony Gyarzalez caught five passes for 100 yards as Mt. Silver beat Petalburg 17–14. Gronkaludon caught all five of his targets for 43 yards while Mossdeep’s wide receivers supplied the fireworks. Those are different jobs inside winning offenses. A tight end can carry a large share of the passing game or keep it functioning around somebody else. The draft mistake is buying the first job, then complaining when the player was selected for the second.

Across the season, Gronkaludon has 39 catches for 452 yards and six touchdowns. Tony has 35 for 440 and two. I would happily build around either kind of production. I would be much less happy promising it from a workout. The grade ranges and combine results below are what we have; they leave room for disagreement about technique, deployment and how quickly a prospect can contribute. I am ranking the six listed tight ends.

Arctozolt is the fastest of the group at 4.87 seconds, but Trubbish creates the most interesting argument after the top two. Cascarrafa’s prospect combines a 4.91 forty with the best cone time here, 6.77, and a 36-inch vertical. That is a much more inviting movement profile than the name might suggest to somebody who scouts the mascot before the player. My board keeps Trubbish third because the 56–84 grade band leaves the stronger present case with Dhelmise and Arctozolt. My curiosity is less obedient.

Fortree would be one of my first stops with this board. An 0–6 team should be interested in adding a receiving outlet who gives the offense another credible job to run. I like Arctozolt there if the asking price fits its eventual draft position; I would take Dhelmise ahead of him if both were available at a sensible price. Those are player-fit opinions. Nobody has assigned the Skyhawks a pick number yet, and a losing record does not make every expensive solution a good purchase.

For a different conversation, take Mauville. Heatmor already has 31 catches for 345 yards. That is useful incumbent production, so I would not walk into that room selling a tight end as the only route to a functional offense. A developmental option could add depth, but the first question is whether the available selection has a better job elsewhere. Calvin Rook can like a prospect without finding thirty-two emergencies for him.

The bottom three require patience, with three quite different reasons for it. Clamperl has the stronger grade band of that group and the slowest movement tests. Sizzlipede offers a better cone result but only six bench reps. Oshawott has the lowest grade range and the best vertical in the class. I would rather be specific about those tradeoffs than hide all three behind the word upside. Their eventual jobs and prices need to reflect what separates them.

prospects.name: Dhelmise
prospects.analysis: Santalune’s Dhelmise gets the first line on my card because the strongest grade range in the class comes with its strongest bench result. Twenty-eight reps do not prove blocking technique, but they give me a concrete physical reason to investigate an attached role. The 5.06 forty and 7.24 cone push me away from selling a space-dominating receiver. I want this prospect near the formation, giving an offense a sturdier starting point and enough receiving ability to make the defense account for him. That is a valuable brief without decorating it with an imaginary college highlight reel.
prospects.concern: The 30-inch vertical and slower cone result leave the receiving ceiling open to debate. At 22, he is also the oldest prospect of these six; I want the present contribution to justify putting him first.
prospects.projection: First tight end on my board. I would have Fortree and Celadon examine whether his strongest projected job fits their offensive rebuilding needs before spending an early selection.

prospects.name: Arctozolt
prospects.analysis: Lavender Forest’s Arctozolt owns the best forty here, 4.87, alongside 20 bench reps and a 67–95 grade range. That is the clearest alternative to Dhelmise if a club wants more speed without abandoning the physical part of the position. Cerulean’s current Arctozolt has 18 catches for 188 yards this season; the shared species makes for an easy introduction, but it does not establish that these are interchangeable players. My case for the prospect comes from his own range and workout. I see the most persuasive balanced profile after the leader.
prospects.concern: A 7.18 cone is substantially slower than Trubbish’s 6.77, and the 31-inch vertical does not separate him from the class. Straight-line speed is only part of the receiving assignment.
prospects.projection: My preferred alternative for Fortree if the offense wants a faster outlet. Second on the board, with a credible argument for first in a room that values that particular job more heavily.

prospects.name: Trubbish
prospects.analysis: Cascarrafa’s Trubbish is the prospect I expect to keep defending after the meeting has technically ended. The 6.77 cone leads the group, the 4.91 forty is second, and the 36-inch vertical adds another attractive movement result. I would start by exploring a receiving role that gives those traits room to matter. The 56–84 grade band is why I stop at third: the workout makes a stronger claim about athletic possibilities than about immediate completeness. That tension is the entire attraction. There is something here to investigate, and I do not need to pretend the investigation is finished.
prospects.concern: Fifteen bench reps trail both leaders. An offense asking him to solve its blocking problems immediately would need firmer evidence than this workout supplies.
prospects.projection: Third overall at the position and my favorite receiving-value discussion if the price drops below the top pair. Celadon would be an interesting fit opinion, not an automatic replacement for its current tight end.

prospects.name: Clamperl
prospects.analysis: Hulbury’s Clamperl is fourth because a 45–73 grade range offers a better present starting point than the final two prospects. The workout is less persuasive: 5.20 in the forty, 7.31 in the cone and a 28-inch vertical are all the slowest or lowest marks in this group. Sixteen bench reps at least keep the physical conversation alive. I would ask a club to describe the actual assignment before falling in love with a later possibility. A shorter-area role and a patient depth plan sound more believable to me than promising a receiver who separates all over the field.
prospects.concern: Every movement comparison places him behind the top three. Future development is a question for the scouting process, not a license to erase today’s tests.
prospects.projection: A later depth consideration for a club that can offer time and a defined job. I would not make an offense counting on an immediate receiving improvement wait on this projection.

prospects.name: Sizzlipede
prospects.analysis: Stow-on-Side State’s Sizzlipede brings a 6.96 cone and 34-inch vertical, enough to make a movement-based role worth discussing at the right price. The grade range is 34–62, and six bench reps make it difficult to present him as a ready answer near the line. I prefer that everybody involved agree on the patience required before the selection is made. The useful version of this pick is a small investment in a specific developmental assignment. The expensive version is a club buying the possibility, then asking him to perform like one of the top two immediately.
prospects.concern: The lowest bench result in this class is an obvious follow-up question. The workout does not tell us enough about functional strength or technique to wave it away.
prospects.projection: Fifth on my board. A depth project for a roster with room to develop a receiving option; I would want a modest acquisition cost and no immediate starting promise.

prospects.name: Oshawott
prospects.analysis: Gateon State’s Oshawott has the best vertical among these tight ends at 37 inches. That earns a real note in the file, alongside a 6.95 cone that is also competitive within this group. It does not erase the lowest grade band, 28–56, or nine bench reps. I am keeping him sixth because the overall present case remains the least convincing, while acknowledging that one good athletic trait can give a development staff something concrete to work on. The argument should begin with the player we can evaluate, then move carefully toward the player a team hopes to have.
prospects.concern: The 5.03 forty is ordinary in this class, and the current grade range leaves considerable work before anyone should promise a reliable IFL role.
prospects.projection: A patient late option if the roster and price allow it. I would choose the defined developmental opportunity over a famous-species comparison, however much better the comparison sounds on television.

articles.title: The correction desk: sixty-three points and several apologies
articles.dek: Mossdeep makes first place easy. Mt. Silver forces Rowan to reconsider, Blackthorn erupts, and Cerulean finally gets the promotion it earned.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: I owe Mt. Silver and Cerulean better rankings. Rustboro would probably prefer I stop helping. This week’s theme is the correction desk, because I put my opinions in permanent print and the league insists on playing more games afterward. Mossdeep remains first after scoring 63. The argument begins at second, where the unbeaten Reds have earned their place back above my favorite defense.

These are my judgments about the teams now, including known absences and the opponents they just faced. Movement compares with the published Week 6 list. Blackthorn makes the largest climb near the top; Lavender takes a hard fall after its first game since the bye. Four clubs were idle, and none gets a fictional result for the convenience of this column.

rankings.text: Eight catches, 233 yards and five touchdowns for Accel BeckhmJr. Mossdeep beat Lavender 63–10 and reached a plus-254 margin. I could invent a clever reason to move the Eclipse down, but even my profession has limits. The bye is the first opponent this month with a reliable method of keeping them off the scoreboard.

I dropped the unbeaten Reds to fourth last week because Josh Alakazam was lost for the season. They answered with a 17–14 win over a good Petalburg side, with Tony Gyarzalez catching five passes for 100 yards. Seven wins have survived a serious change at quarterback. My caution was reasonable. My ranking was too low.

rankings.themeLabel: A quiet promotion for somebody else
rankings.text: The Psi Corps did nothing wrong on their bye. Mt. Silver did something right, so Saffron slides one place. Thirty-four points allowed across six games remains a tremendous argument. Pastoria next gives Trent Scarboro a chance to pair that defense with an offense more persuasive than the one that escaped Fuchsia.

Hatterene completed 30 of 35 passes for 410 yards and five touchdowns in a 42–0 win. Yes, it was Lavaridge. No, that does not make those completions disappear. I had the 5–1 Dragons eleventh; this correction is overdue. Lavender arrives next, and its last opponent has helpfully demonstrated the value of attacking through the air.

rankings.themeLabel: Keep the receipt, lower the volume
rankings.text: Seven points were enough against Eterna. That makes the Blaze 5–2 with a plus-58 margin, which is substantial; it also makes Dorian’s next declaration of offensive supremacy an interesting editing assignment. I am holding Cinnabar fifth because the season is better than this single scoring line. Mauville will ask for a little more.

DeZhaun Watzon went 10-for-26 for 125 yards and an interception in a 12–6 loss at Cerulean. Last week’s return touchdowns cannot keep contributing after the week ends, a scheduling detail my previous third-place ranking overlooked. The Starseekers still own a plus-89 margin. I am docking the offense, not confiscating the first five wins.

Losing 17–14 at Mt. Silver does not send a 5–2 team tumbling down this list. It does keep the Pride behind the teams I trust to finish that game. The bye arrives with Vileplume and Venomoth still carrying remaining absences. Petalburg gets a week to recover while its ranking does considerably less moving than my eyebrows.

rankings.themeLabel: I would prefer to be wrong
rankings.text: Drakloak caught four passes for 149 yards in a 14–9 win over Hearthome. The Volts are 5–1, and I have run out of ways to describe that as an administrative accident. Tentacruel’s five-week absence adds another problem at corner. For now, the league’s leading receiver keeps giving this restrained offense a very loud escape route.

The Tide held Sunyshore to six points and won 12–6. I had them twenty-third. Please direct complaints to last week’s Rowan, who seems poorly informed and annoyingly confident. Cerulean is 4–3 despite a minus-23 margin; I am not erasing the ugly afternoons. I am finally charging enough for the good ones.

The Bulwark have outscored their opponents 90–89 and somehow turned that into 5–2. A 9–7 victory at Celadon fits the collection. Slowking completed eight of nine passes for 142 yards and a touchdown, so the offense can be efficient without being busy. I respect the record; I would like its emergency fund to contain more than one point.

A 10–7 win over Snowpoint brings the Titans to 4–3 and plus-seven. That earns a climb in a middle class determined to make rankings labor-intensive. Losing Toucannon for eight weeks is the obvious concern before Rustboro visits. The result deserves credit, while the injury makes it harder to assume the defense will simply repeat itself.

Beating Dewford 17–14 moves the Ironclads to 3–3. Drampa threw two touchdowns without an interception; Grotle supplied five catches for 50 yards and a score. I am promoting a team that handled a direct comparison well. A trip to Eterna will establish whether this is a useful new address or a one-week rental.

Mahogany edged winless Fortree 14–13 and remains plus-21 despite a 3–4 record. That margin keeps me interested, although surviving this opponent by one point is an odd way to reward the attention. Dugtrio is out two weeks. The Frost now visit Sunyshore, where both teams have a passing-game argument they would like to settle.

rankings.themeLabel: Defense cannot order the whole meal
rankings.text: Three points at Cinnabar spoiled a defensive effort that allowed seven. The Thorns have scored 60 and allowed 58 across six games; being 3–3 is almost excessively literal. Trevenant and Aipom each face a one-week absence. I still trust enough of the defense to keep Eterna here. I would trust it more with help.

I moved Rustboro from twentieth to eighth after the Dewford win. Azalea promptly won 14–10, demonstrating why two kickoff touchdowns make an unstable foundation for a ranking. My Way, Son still ran for 109 yards, and Gengar caught five for 80. There is useful offense here. I have stopped handing it a victory before it scores enough.

The Swarm beat Rustboro 14–10, with Vivillon turning four catches into 96 yards and a touchdown. That is a meaningful win for a 3–4 side whose minus-45 margin still argues for restraint. Cianwood comes next. Azalea has earned the opportunity to build on a result; it has not yet earned the right to treat the next one as routine.

rankings.themeLabel: My favorite is costing me ink
rankings.text: A 17–14 loss at Olivine leaves the Breakers 3–4. I kept them ninth after the Rustboro defeat because I thought the underlying team deserved patience. At some point patience becomes an unpaid public-relations job. Excadrill remains out two weeks. Hosting Pewter is a reasonable opportunity to show that the floor is higher than this fortnight suggests.

rankings.themeLabel: The bye gets an ordinary grade
rankings.text: The Surge remain 3–3, with 106 points scored and 146 allowed. A week without a game does not repair that gap, and their next trip to Violet will be a useful comparison between teams trying to escape the lower half. I am leaving room for improvement without awarding advance credit for an opponent they have not beaten yet.

Sixty-three points allowed is a very large complication for a team that entered the week 4–1. The Wails still hold a playoff place, so this is not a funeral. It is a demand for a response, preferably before Blackthorn’s passing game gets comfortable. I had Lavender tenth; the next ranking will depend on whether this becomes a pattern.

Mauville won 17–3 at Cianwood and rises to 3–4. Dragapult supplied 217 passing yards while the defense kept the Crushers to three points. I am giving the Dynamos credit without pretending that a minus-33 season margin has vanished. Cinnabar is a sterner test, and an excellent place to prove this was the beginning of something.

The Blizzard have a positive point differential and a 2–5 record. Losing 10–7 to Viridian is another entry in that deeply unhelpful portfolio. I cannot keep ranking the sum of their scores above the results indefinitely. A visit to unbeaten Mt. Silver is a difficult place to discover how to turn the final three points in their favor.

Violet had the week off and remains 2–4. Sootopolis visits next, giving the Falcons an immediate chance to improve against a team with its own defensive questions. Delibird and Axew still have remaining absences. I am keeping the Falcons above several teams that actively made their cases worse, which is the modest privilege of a well-timed bye.

A 16–13 loss gave Fuchsia its first win and left the Fists 3–4. Thirteen points against a defense that entered the week having allowed 156 is a poor return on the opportunity. Oreburgh comes next. I want a more forceful offensive answer before I start treating that three-win record as evidence of anything comfortable.

The Miners won 13–6 at Pewter and have reached 2–5. It is not a glamorous score, but teams at this end of the rankings cannot afford to review victories for aesthetic defects. Farigiraf has one week remaining on the injury list. Veilstone provides a chance to make the improvement consecutive, which is where I start paying closer attention.

Pastoria remains 2–4 after a bye and now visits Saffron. Oinkologne still has seven weeks remaining on the injury report. I do not like that combination against a defense allowing fewer than six points per game. There is no penalty for an idle week here; there is simply very little new reason to feel more ambitious.

Empoleon completed 22 of 29 passes for 212 yards and a touchdown as the Shadows beat Veilstone 16–13. After running Saffron close, Fuchsia has finally turned encouragement into a win. The minus-94 margin still belongs on the page. So does 1–6, and a home game with Celadon now looks like an opportunity rather than another appointment to dread.

The Haunts lost 14–9 at Vermilion, then emerged with an eight-week absence for Luxray. At 2–5, with Luvdisc also unavailable, Hearthome has to find more offense from a narrowing selection of options. Canalave is next. A close loss can establish competitiveness; the Haunts need to establish an actual supply of points.

rankings.themeLabel: The museum has a medical wing
rankings.text: Six points at home against Oreburgh takes the Rockers to 3–4. Gurdurr joins the current absences with two weeks to miss. I would ordinarily make a joke about six points being an exhibit, but Dewford is approaching and Pewter needs an offense that travels better than this. The season total is 57. There is the exhibit.

A 17–3 defeat is bad enough. Losing Gardevoir for ten weeks changes what comes after it. The Crushers are 2–5 and now head to Azalea with a serious quarterback problem. This ranking reflects that immediate outlook as well as the result. I am much less interested in assigning blame than in seeing where the next touchdown comes from.

Celadon allowed nine points and still lost. That sentence explains why a respectable 90 points conceded has produced a 1–6 record: the Bloom have scored 58. Fuchsia is next, newly acquainted with winning and unlikely to offer sympathy. I am resisting the temptation to reward another narrow defeat. Celadon already has quite a collection.

A 14–13 loss at Mahogany keeps Fortree at 0–6. I can acknowledge the better score without pretending the missing victory is a formatting error. Vermilion visits next, bringing Drakloak and a 5–1 record. The Skyhawks need one afternoon in which their competitiveness survives all the way into the standings.

Forty-two points allowed, none scored. The Inferno have given up 203 points in seven games and are minus-125. A bye is welcome because repeating either side of this performance would be difficult to explain. I had Lavaridge last a week ago. Sometimes the easiest ranking on the page is also the least pleasant one to write.

articles.title: Week 8: Lavender faces the next storm, Sunyshore looks for its answer
articles.dek: Tessa owns the Week 7 misses, grades her keys and calls all fourteen games as Saffron returns and Mossdeep rests.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Ellis won Week 7 at 10–4. Dorian and I went 8–6, Mara finished 7–7, and Rowan went 5–9. Across all three graded weeks, Dorian leads at 28–15, followed by me at 25–18, Rowan at 23–20, Ellis at 22–21 and Mara at 21–22. I have asked Ellis to enjoy his weekly victory quietly enough that the rest of us can finish our corrections. Closest-score bonuses are separate: he added five, Mara four, Rowan and Dorian two apiece, and I added one.

My Mossdeep forecast was right about the winner and thoroughly wrong about the scale. I asked Lavender for three punts and no completion of thirty yards or more; Accel BeckhmJr's fifty-five-yard catch alone settles the second test. I asked the Eclipse to allow at most one sack and finish three touchdown drives. They allowed two sacks and scored nine touchdowns. Rustboro reached my 150-yard rushing threshold exactly and lost. Those are useful reminders to grade the actual keys instead of quietly replacing them with a checkmark beside the winner.

Week 8 sends Lavender to a Blackthorn offense fresh from 42 points, brings Saffron back from its bye, and gives Sunyshore a home chance to answer its six-point loss. Mossdeep, Cerulean, Petalburg and Lavaridge are off. Fourteen games mean seventy panel forecasts, and no refuge for Rowan in an abbreviated slate. The new injuries matter most in Cianwood, Viridian and Mahogany; all three are trying to replace production that was visible last week.

matchups.matchup: Drakloak against a defense trying to buy Fortree its first win
matchups.analysis: Vermilion is 5–1 with only 82 points scored. That is an unusually narrow road to a good record, and Fortree nearly closed its own losing streak in a 14–13 defeat at Mahogany. Drakloak gives the Volts an escape route: four catches produced 149 yards last week. I favor that receiving threat, while the absences of cornerbacks Tentacruel and Delcatty give Fortree a plausible answer through the air.
matchups.awayKey: Allow fewer than two passing touchdowns and commit no turnovers.
matchups.homeKey: Complete three passes of at least twenty yards and lose no fumbles.

matchups.matchup: Two ground games, and a missing Eterna receiving option
matchups.analysis: Olivine ran for 112 yards and allowed no sacks in its 17–14 win over Dewford. Eterna ran for 113 and still scored only three at Cinnabar. The Thorns' missing tight end Trevenant makes finishing possessions harder; linebacker Aipom is also out. I lean narrowly toward Eterna's defense at home. A team that has allowed 58 points in six games deserves that much trust, even when its offense makes the trust uncomfortable.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no more than one sack and turn two possessions into touchdowns.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Olivine below one hundred rushing yards and score a first-half touchdown.

matchups.matchup: Lavender’s coverage after the worst possible rehearsal
matchups.analysis: Lavender gave up five receiving touchdowns to Accel BeckhmJr. Now Hatterene awaits after throwing for 410 yards and five touchdowns against Lavaridge, with Ninjask catching seven for 183. This is an unpleasant change of address for Travis Scarboro's defense. Blackthorn corner Hawlucha is out, but Mr. Clanky's twelve completions in 34 attempts do not yet justify predicting a shootout. I expect a better Wails performance and another Dragons win.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no reception longer than thirty yards and throw no interceptions.
matchups.homeKey: Complete at least sixty-five percent of passes and force three punts.

matchups.matchup: Saffron’s rested defense against an attack missing its halfback
matchups.analysis: The Psi Corps return at 5–1 with 34 points allowed across six games. Pastoria is 2–4 and still missing Oinkologne, whose injury carries seven weeks remaining. Saffron also lacks fullback Vigoroth, so I am not forecasting an effortless offensive afternoon. Trent Scarboro's defense should make the difference. Pastoria needs repeated ordinary completions to keep this from becoming a succession of obvious passing downs.
matchups.awayKey: Convert at least five third downs and surrender no defensive touchdowns.
matchups.homeKey: Record at least three sacks and commit no more than one turnover.

matchups.matchup: Two rested teams with very little margin for another stumble
matchups.analysis: Sootopolis is 3–3 despite allowing forty more points than it has scored. Violet is 2–4 and down thirty-one. Neither record invites a grand declaration, especially after both teams had the week off. Violet remains without receiver Delibird and defensive end Axew. I give the Surge a small edge, while requiring more than its last win over Fortree to believe the offense has solved anything permanently.
matchups.awayKey: Score on at least three possessions and allow no return touchdown.
matchups.homeKey: Keep Sootopolis below 120 rushing yards and win the turnover margin.

matchups.matchup: Snowpoint’s scoring drought against another Reds quarterback test
matchups.analysis: Mt. Silver stayed unbeaten by holding Petalburg to fourteen while Porygon-Z threw two touchdowns. Tony Gyarzalez's five catches for one hundred yards supplied a dependable target. Snowpoint managed seven points at Viridian and now meets a defense allowing 59 through seven games. I expect the Reds to make enough stops to spare their new quarterback an afternoon of rescue work. Josh Alakazam and Garshawn Lynch remain out; seven wins have not healed either injury.
matchups.awayKey: Hold Mt. Silver below twenty points and finish two touchdown drives.
matchups.homeKey: Allow no more than two sacks and hold Snowpoint below 250 total yards.

matchups.matchup: A damaged Frost running game against Watzon’s response
matchups.analysis: Sunyshore's six points in Cerulean came with ten completions in 26 attempts from DeZhaun Watzon. Karson Jones needs a much steadier passing day. Mahogany won by one while running for 151 yards, but Dugtrio is now out for two weeks after contributing 53 of those yards. I favor a home response from the Starseekers. The Frost's plus-twenty-one scoring margin makes them a credible visitor, not a convenient recovery appointment.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for at least 120 yards and prevent a return touchdown.
matchups.homeKey: Complete at least sixty percent of passes and take no more than two sacks.

matchups.matchup: Unfezant’s running against a thinning Pewter defense
matchups.analysis: Dewford gained 122 rushing yards without taking a sack in Olivine, then lost because that production did not buy enough points. Frosmoth's two interceptions matter. Pewter's six-point afternoon offers room to survive another imperfect performance, and its defense now lacks Gurdurr as well as cornerbacks Scolipede and Venusaur. I like Unfezant to give the Breakers manageable possessions. I would like the quarterback to leave both teams' defenders out of the distribution list.
matchups.awayKey: Hold Dewford below 110 rushing yards and score a touchdown before halftime.
matchups.homeKey: Throw no interceptions and produce two touchdown drives.

matchups.matchup: Rustboro’s rushing production against Viridian’s new linebacker loss
matchups.analysis: Rustboro reached 150 rushing yards at Azalea and still lost 14–10. That is a finishing problem Tyler Scarboro can take into a matchup with a Viridian defense now missing Toucannon for eight weeks. The Titans won while throwing for only 103 yards. I prefer the Stone's broader offensive output, with Gengar's five catches for eighty providing another route when the run slows. Parasect remains out for Rustboro, so the middle is vulnerable on both sides.
matchups.awayKey: Score touchdowns on two red-zone visits and lose no fumbles.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for one hundred yards and hold Rustboro below twenty points.

matchups.matchup: Mauville’s volume against the Blaze’s patient passing game
matchups.analysis: Cinnabar won 7–3, a score that does little advertising for an offense with Gholdengo, Exploud and Beautifly. Mauville's Dragapult attempted 42 passes in a 17–3 win over Cianwood. I expect the Blaze to make those possessions less comfortable, while Exploud's seven catches for 66 offer a way to stay on the field. The Dynamos can win if they turn volume into touchdowns; I currently trust Cinnabar's defense more than that conversion.
matchups.awayKey: Throw at least two touchdown passes and take no more than two sacks.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Mauville below twenty points and complete four passes to Exploud.

matchups.matchup: Canalave’s narrow wins meet an injured Hearthome backfield
matchups.analysis: The Bulwark are 5–2 with ninety points scored and 89 allowed. The record is real; the cushion is not. Hearthome has just lost halfback Luxray for eight weeks and remains without slot receiver Luvdisc. Canalave ran for 112 yards in Celadon, so I favor the home side to keep this small and win another close one. Four sacks allowed last week are the quickest way for that plan to unravel.
matchups.awayKey: Sack the quarterback three times and finish two touchdown drives.
matchups.homeKey: Allow no more than two sacks and run for at least one hundred yards.

matchups.matchup: Cianwood’s quarterback vacancy against a three-win Swarm surge
matchups.analysis: Cianwood's Gardevoir is out for ten weeks. Wigglytuff completed seven of thirteen passes for 93 yards and an interception in the loss to Mauville, leaving the Crushers with an urgent offensive adjustment. Azalea has won three straight, most recently while allowing Rustboro plenty of yardage but only ten points. Scraggy's absence weakens the Swarm's linebackers; I still prefer their continuity at quarterback and Vivillon's receiving threat.
matchups.awayKey: Lose no fumbles and score at least ten points before halftime.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Cianwood below 250 yards and complete two touchdown passes.

matchups.matchup: A modest passing contest with little room for a giveaway
matchups.analysis: Oreburgh finally won again, beating Pewter 13–6 as Cryogonal completed twelve of fourteen passes. Veilstone lost at Fuchsia with only 98 passing yards from Tatsugiri. Neither showing promises a large score. I give the Fists a narrow home edge, but Oreburgh's efficient short passing could reverse that if the protection improves from three sacks allowed. Farigiraf is still unavailable for the Miners, while Veilstone remains without Kricketune.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no more than one sack and finish two touchdown drives.
matchups.homeKey: Pass for at least 150 yards and throw no interceptions.

matchups.matchup: Empoleon’s completions against Celadon’s improving resistance
matchups.analysis: Two 1–6 teams can still play a consequential game for themselves. Fuchsia's first victory came with 22 completions in 29 attempts from Empoleon; Celadon followed its own first win with a 9–7 loss to Canalave. The Bloom allowed 112 rushing yards but kept Canalave to nine points. Fuchsia will need to turn its passing production into finished drives, and Seaking's seven catches give me a reason to pick the Shadows. Celadon has kept two straight opponents to ten or fewer and deserves more than a dismissal.
matchups.awayKey: Allow fewer than two passing touchdowns and gain seventy rushing yards.
matchups.homeKey: Complete at least twenty passes and allow no defensive or return touchdown.
